St. Symeon the New Theologian

St. Symeon the New Theologian

St. Simeon the New Theologian

Period

Region

Titles / vocation
Monastic
Commemoration

Introduction

St. Symeon, rendered Simeon on the cited page, is remembered as a monk and spiritual writer associated with Constantinople. The life distinguishes him from his elder Simeon the Pious and identifies Nicetas Stethatos as his biographer. It also notes the transfer of his feast from March 12 to October 12 because of Lent. The displayed date follows this source entry rather than overriding parish practice.

Read circumstances and sources

Background

Benedict XVI’s biographical address describes Symeon’s education in Constantinople and his turn from a projected public career toward monastic life. It identifies Symeon the Pious as his spiritual guide and connects his reading of ascetical authors with the experience later described in his writings. This is a modern Roman Catholic account of an Eastern saint, used here for identified biographical context, not as an Orthodox jurisdictional pronouncement.

[2] Official ecclesiastical biography or biographical address · Biographical reading / named life section

Life and notable events

The biographical address distinguishes the Studite monastery, his move to Saint Mamas, and his eventual leadership there. It connects difficulties at the Studion with his unusual devotion to his elder and his mystical experiences. It also records rehabilitation by Patriarch Sergius II after exile, and places much of his later writing at Saint Marina. These details give the institutional setting for a life remembered principally through his teachings and his disciple’s biography.

[2] Official ecclesiastical biography or biographical address · Biographical reading / named life section

At Saint Mamas, St. Symeon’s reform met resistance and an attack by some monks; the Life says he sought leniency for them. He later resigned the abbacy to write. Conflict with ecclesiastical authorities led to banishment across the Bosphorus and continued monastic life.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life; biographical narrative and concluding account

Death and martyrdom

The OCA Life dates peaceful repose to 1021; GOARCH uses 1022. His March 12 repose is distinguished from the October 12 feast transferred to avoid Lent.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life; biographical narrative and concluding account · [3] Official ecclesiastical biography or biographical address · GOARCH October 12 reading; death chronology

Writings and legacy

GOARCH places Symeon with St. John the Evangelist and Gregory among the saints called Theologian. It associates this title with his teaching and life; it is not an academic degree.

[3] Official ecclesiastical biography or biographical address · Biographical reading / named life section

The address identifies Nicetas Stethatos as the best-known disciple who preserved Symeon’s writings and compiled his posthumous Life. It also distinguishes catecheses, treatises, and hymns rather than treating every text circulated under his name as the same work. The disciple’s relationship to the saint matters when reading that Life as an attributed witness.

[2] Official ecclesiastical biography or biographical address · Biographical reading / named life section
